mainTopic: Levite city houses that are sold, and a כהן who consecrates his שדה חרם: does it come back to him at the יובל?
overview: The amud opens at the end of a ברייתא about houses of the לויים in a walled city. The גמרא objects that a city of the לויים may not keep its wall anyway. רב אשי answers that the rule is still needed for the time before the wall comes down, so a לוי's sold house can always be redeemed. Then a new ברייתא explains the words 'כשדה החרם' (ויקרא 27:21). A כהן who consecrates a field he received as חרם might argue with a כל שכן that it should stay his at the יובל, but the פסוק rejects this. Using בא ללמד ונמצא למד, the ברייתא shows that his field, like an Israelite's consecrated ancestral field, is divided among all the כהנים. The גמרא then asks why the פסוק was needed at all, since the כהן's כל שכן is weak. רמי בר חמא suggests a comparison to a כהן's own קדשים, which the גמרא rejects. רב נחמן answers that the word 'אחוזתו' shows that only a כהן's inherited field is his lasting possession, not his חרם field. The amud ends with the Hadran closing the chapter הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ and all of מסכת ערכין.

steps.title: Walls of a Levite city must come down anyway
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by saying the Levite houses and their open lots count as a walled city. The גמרא objects that these walls are going to be torn down anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: 'both they and their open lots.' The גמרא asks: but they and their lots are going to be torn down!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last words of a ברייתא about Levite houses in a walled city. It then challenges how such a city can be treated as walled at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Levite city is not allowed to stay surrounded by a wall, so the wall is going to be removed. If the wall will not last, why does the ברייתא bother discussing the rules of a walled city here? The challenge is that the case seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: The open land around a Levite city
The cities given to the Levites
They stand to be torn down
Houses in walled cities, which can only be redeemed within one year of being sold

phrases.english: Both they and their open lots.
phrases.notes: These are the last words of the ברייתא from the previous daf about Levite houses in a walled city.

phrases.english: But they and their lots stand to be torn down!
phrases.notes: A Levite city may not keep a wall around it, so the wall is going to come down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of the ברייתא from the previous daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's treatment of a Levite city as a walled city
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The walls must be torn down, so treating the city as walled seems meaningless.

steps.title: רב אשי: the rule is needed while the wall still stands
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the ברייתא still needed to teach the rule. Otherwise we might think that while the wall is standing, a sale becomes permanent like any walled-city house.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It was needed. You might have thought: when the walls are torn down, they are torn down, but until then, if the houses are sold, they become the buyer's forever. So the ברייתא teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the challenge by showing what mistake the ברייתא prevents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the wall is removed, the city looks like a regular walled city. In a regular walled city, an unredeemed house becomes the buyer's forever after one year. The ברייתא teaches that a Levite house can still always be redeemed, even during that time.

keyTerms.meaning: It was necessary to teach this
It could have entered your mind to say
Let them become the buyer's permanently
This teaches us

steps.whatToRemember: Even while its wall still stands, a Levite city does not follow the walled-city rule. A Levite's sold house can always be redeemed.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: It was necessary;
it could have entered your mind to say:
When they are torn down, they are torn down;
but if they are sold in the meantime, let them belong to the buyer forever.
phrases.notes: He means after the one-year redemption period passes, like any house in a walled city.

phrases.english: So it teaches us that this is not so.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the rule is needed for the time before the wall is removed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: While the wall stands, a sold Levite house becomes the buyer's forever after a year.
steps.terutzMaskana: A Levite house can always be redeemed, even while the wall still stands.

steps.title: Why the Torah says 'like a dedicated field'
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא asks what the words 'כשדה החרם' come to teach. It applies them to a כהן who consecrated a field he had received as חרם, and who might claim the field should stay his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'As a dedicated field, his ancestral field shall be the priest's.' What does this teach? From where do we learn that a כהן who consecrated his חרם field may not say: 'Since such a field goes out to the כהנים, and it is already in my hands, it should be mine'?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The ברייתא sets up a case and a claim that the פסוק will later reject.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A consecrated field that is not redeemed goes to the כהנים at the יובל. A כהן who consecrated his own חרם field argues that since he is a כהן and already holds the field, it should simply stay with him. The ברייתא says the פסוק's words 'כשדה החרם' are there to reject this claim.

keyTerms.meaning: A field that an Israelite dedicated to the כהנים
Consecrated something to the בית המקדש
What does the פסוק come to teach?
The fiftieth year, when fields return to their owners
In my possession

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"As a dedicated field, his ancestral field shall be the priest's"
What does the verse come to teach?
From where do we learn that a priest who consecrated his dedicated field
phrases.notes: 'His dedicated field' means a field an Israelite gave to this כהן as חרם.

phrases.english: may not say: Since it goes out to the priests at the Jubilee,

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲרֵי הִיא תַּחַת יָדִי — תְּהֵא שֶׁלִּי.
phrases.english: and here it is in my hands, let it be mine.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״כִּשְׂדֵה הַחֵרֶם לַכֹּהֵן תִּהְיֶה אֲחֻזָּתוֹ״, מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא on a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן who consecrated his חרם field may not keep it for himself at the יובל.

steps.title: The כהן's 'all the more so' argument
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא spells out the כהן's argument as a כל שכן: if I can acquire other people's consecrated fields, surely I can acquire my own.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it seems logical: if I acquire fields that belonged to others, should I not all the more so acquire my own?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא presents the strong logic behind the כהן's claim. This sets up the פסוק that will reject it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Other people's unredeemed consecrated fields go to the כהנים at the יובל. So the כהן reasons that a field he himself consecrated should surely stay with him. This is a קל וחומר that seems hard to refute without a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: It is logical (a reasoned argument)
All the more so
Acquires

phrases.english: And it seems logical:
With fields of others, I acquire them;
with my own, is it not all the more so?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִין הוּא: בְּשֶׁל אֲחֵרִים אֲנִי זוֹכֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the claim described in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the כהן loses his consecrated חרם field
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר: if he acquires other people's fields, he should surely keep his own.

steps.title: The פסוק rejects the כהן's argument
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings the פסוק 'when it goes out in the יובל, holy to ה׳, like a dedicated field' to show that the כהן's logic is wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק therefore says: 'And the field, when it goes out in the יובל, shall be holy to ה׳, like a dedicated field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the כל שכן with a פסוק. The Torah decides the case, not the logic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'כשדה החרם' tie the כהן's case to the rule of an ordinary consecrated field. That is why his קל וחומר does not work. The next steps explain exactly how this comparison works.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore the פסוק says
When it goes out in the יובל
Holy to ה׳

phrases.english: Therefore the verse says:
"And the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee,
shall be holy to ה׳, like a dedicated field."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קל וחומר of step 4 with a פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A פסוק overrides the logical argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The כהן keeps his own consecrated חרם field because of the כל שכן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק links his field to 'שדה החרם', so he does not keep it.

steps.title: What did we ever learn about a dedicated field?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how the פסוק can compare to 'a dedicated field' when we have not yet learned any rule about a dedicated field.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what have we learned from the dedicated field up to now?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a puzzle about how the comparison works. It is setting up its explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you compare a new case to a case whose law you already know. Here the Torah says 'like a dedicated field', but no rule about a dedicated field has been stated. So what are we being compared to?

keyTerms.meaning: Up to now; so far
But what have we learned?

phrases.english: But what have we learned
from the dedicated field so far?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מָה לָמַדְנוּ מִשְּׂדֵה הַחֵרֶם מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the פסוק quoted in step 5 can work as a comparison.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What known rule about a שדה חרם the comparison draws on

steps.title: The comparison works both ways
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that the חרם case 'comes to teach and ends up learning'. The פסוק compares the כהן's חרם field to an Israelite's ancestral field: both leave the holder's hands and are divided among the כהנים.
steps.simpleTranslation: This case came to teach and turns out to learn. The verse compares the כהן's dedicated field to an Israelite's ancestral field. Just as an Israelite's ancestral field leaves the holder's hands and is divided among the כהנים, so too the כהן's dedicated field leaves his hands and is divided among his brothers, the כהנים.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains that the comparison goes in both directions. This gives the final rule for the כהן's field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'כשדה החרם' looks like it teaches about the ancestral field, but it also learns from it (בא ללמד ונמצא למד). An Israelite's consecrated field, even when a כהן redeemed it, goes out of his hands at the יובל and is split among all the כהנים. The same happens to the כהן's own consecrated חרם field, so his כל שכן fails.

keyTerms.meaning: Comes to teach and turns out to learn: the comparison works both ways
Compares one case to another based on a פסוק (הֶקֵּשׁ)
An ancestral field that came to a family by inheritance
Is divided among the כהנים

steps.whatToRemember: A כהן who consecrates a field he got as חרם does not get it back at the יובל. Like an Israelite's consecrated ancestral field, it is divided among all the כהנים, because the פסוק compares the two cases in both directions.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Comes to teach and turns out to learn' does not mean the פסוק teaches nothing about the ancestral field. It teaches in both directions: each case gets something from the other.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two-way comparison is what defeats the כהן's כל שכן. It shows that a הקש from the Torah can override logical reasoning.

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי זֶה בָּא לְלַמֵּד וְנִמְצָא לָמֵד,
phrases.english: This came to teach and turns out to learn:

phrases.aramaic: מַקִּישׁ שְׂדֵה חֶרְמוֹ לִשְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: it compares his dedicated field to the ancestral field of an Israelite.
Just as the ancestral field of an Israelite
leaves his hands and is divided among the priests,
phrases.notes: 'His hands' means the כהן who redeemed that field from הקדש.

phrases.aramaic: אַף שְׂדֵה חֶרְמוֹ יוֹצָא מִתַּחַת יָדוֹ
phrases.english: so too, his dedicated field leaves his hands
and is divided among his brothers, the priests.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי זֶה בָּא לְלַמֵּד וְנִמְצָא לָמֵד
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The comparison is two-way. The כהן's חרם field learns from the Israelite's ancestral field and is divided among all the כהנים.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A כהן's consecrated חרם field leaves his possession at the יובל and is divided among all the כהנים.

steps.title: The כהן's argument does not really work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the כהן's argument from the ברייתא and attacks it. Getting a share of someone else's field is not like taking your own field back completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'I acquire the fields of others.' Are these the same? There he just gets a share. Here he is taking the whole field for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the כהן's כל שכן from the ברייתא and shows it is weak. So why would the פסוק need to reject it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: With other people's consecrated fields, the כהן is only one of many כהנים who share the field. Here he wants the whole field back for himself alone. That is a much bigger claim, so the כל שכן falls apart, and the פסוק seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: Are these really alike? A way of challenging a comparison.
He merely acquires a share, along with others.
He takes it for himself, all of it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר: בְּשֶׁל אֲחֵרִים אֲנִי זוֹכֶה.
phrases.english: The Master said: In the fields of others, I acquire.
phrases.notes: This quotes the כהן's argument from the ברייתא in Step 4.

phrases.english: Are these comparable?
There, he merely acquires a share,
here, he takes it all for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the כל שכן in Step 4 and questions whether it was a real argument at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The כהן's כל שכן in the ברייתא, and so the need for the פסוק to reject it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two cases are not alike. Sharing in others' fields is a small right, but taking your own field back whole is a big one. The smaller case cannot prove the bigger one.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא: we might compare it to a כהן's own offerings
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא says the פסוק is needed. Otherwise we might think the field is like a כהן's own קדשים, which he keeps for himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: It was needed. You might have thought that since it is written 'and a man's holy things shall be his', this field is also like his holy things.
steps.whatsHappening: רמי בר חמא defends the ברייתא. He gives a different reason someone might think the כהן keeps the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן who brings his own offering keeps its כהן portions for himself. One might think a field he consecrated is also 'his holy thing' and so goes back to him. The פסוק teaches that this is wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed. The teaching is not extra.
You might have thought. This introduces a mistaken idea the source comes to block.
His holy things, meaning offerings that a כהן brings himself.

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said: It was necessary,
as it might enter your mind to say:
since it is written
"And a man's holy things shall be his,"
this too is like his holy things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 8 by giving a new reason why the פסוק is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New mistaken idea (סלקא דעתך) that the פסוק comes to block
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a כהן keeps his own קדשים, a field he consecrated might also go back to him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches that the חרם field does not go back to him.

steps.title: Offerings are not the same as owning a field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רמי בר חמא's comparison. A כהן's offerings are not in his ownership, but here he wants the field back in his ownership.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are these the same? His holy things are not in his ownership. Here, the field would be in his ownership.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רמי בר חמא's answer. Nobody would make that mistake, because the cases are too different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The portions a כהן eats from his own offering are not his property. He gets them as a כהן, in return for the service. Taking a field back means real private ownership, so the comparison to קדשים fails, and the question from Step 8 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: In his ownership, his private property.

phrases.english: Are these comparable?
His holy things are not in his ownership,
here, it would be in his ownership.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רמי בר חמא's whole reason for why the פסוק is needed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: קדשים never become the כהן's private property, but the field would. So the comparison does not hold.

steps.title: רב נחמן: we might call it his lasting possession
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says the פסוק is needed. Otherwise we might think a כהן's חרם field counts as his 'lasting possession', like his inherited field. The word 'אחוזתו' teaches that only his inherited field has that status, not his חרם field.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said: It was needed. You might have thought that since it is written 'for it is a lasting possession for them', this field is also his possession. So the פסוק teaches 'his possession': his inherited field, yes; his חרם field, no.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives a new answer to Step 8 and reads a word in the פסוק closely. This is the last answer in this part of the sugya.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fields of כהנים and לויים are called a 'lasting possession', so they can always be redeemed. One might think a חרם field the כהן received also counts. The word 'אחוזתו' limits this to the field he inherited from his father. A חרם field he consecrated goes out to the כהנים at the יובל.

keyTerms.meaning: A lasting possession, a field that always stays with its family.
It teaches us. This introduces what the source actually shows.
His ancestral field, the land he inherited.
His חרם field, a field given to him as a כהן.

steps.whatToRemember: A כהן's inherited field is his 'lasting possession'. A field he received as חרם is not. If he consecrates it, it goes out to all the כהנים at the יובל.
steps.confusionAlert: רב נחמן does not say the חרם field is not really the כהן's. He only says it does not get the special 'lasting possession' status of an inherited field.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Naḥman said: It was necessary,
as it might enter your mind to say:
since it is written
"For it is a lasting possession for them,"
this too is his possession,
so it teaches us "his ancestral field":
his ancestral field, yes; his dedicated field, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer rejected in Step 10 with a new answer to Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New mistaken idea, blocked by reading a word in the פסוק closely
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A כהן's חרם field might count as his 'lasting possession', like his inherited field.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'אחוזתו' limits that status to his inherited field. A חרם field he consecrated goes out to the כהנים at the יובל.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains why the ברייתא's פסוק is needed and fixes the rule: a חרם field a כהן consecrates does not go back to him.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter and the tractate
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the traditional Hadran farewell to the chapter הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ and announces that מסכת ערכין is complete.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'One who sells his field', and with this מסכת ערכין is finished.
steps.whatsHappening: There is no new argument here. The גמרא is formally closing the chapter הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ and the whole מסכת ערכין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every chapter of the גמרא ends with 'הדרן עלך' plus the chapter's name, which is taken from its opening words. Because this is the last chapter, the line adds that the מסכת itself is done. No new chapter or משנה follows.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you': the farewell formula said at the end of every chapter
'One who sells his field': the name of this chapter, taken from its first words
'It is finished / it has come to an end'
The tractate about vowing a person's set value to the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: The chapter הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ, and all of מסכת ערכין, ends with רב נחמן's teaching: only a כהן's inherited field counts as his 'אחוזה', not a field that came to him through חרם.

phrases.english: We will return to you, 'One who sells his field',
phrases.notes: This is the name of the chapter, taken from its opening words. We are saying goodbye to it and hoping to learn it again.

phrases.english: and Tractate Arakhin is finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the chapter right after רב נחמן's final answer in Step 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter הַמּוֹכֵר שָׂדֵהוּ and מסכת ערכין are complete.
